'''3†.''' To warp.
{{smaller block|Because it ''twineth'' and casteth not, it is passing good for hinges and hookes, for sawne bords, for ledges in dores and gates.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xvi. 40.}}}}
'''4.''' To make turns or flexures; wind; meander.
{{smaller block|As rivers, though they bend and ''twine''.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nae gowden stream thro’ myrtles ''twines''.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', On Pastoral Poetry.}}}}

'''twine<sup>2</sup>''' (twīn), ''v.'' [Var. of ''twin''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To separate; divide; part.
{{smaller block|<poem>And sighing says this lady fair,
“They shou’d gar twa loves ''twine''.”</poem>
{{right|''The Water o’ Wearie’s Well'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 200).}}}}
'''2†.''' To turn.
{{smaller block|<poem>She shrikes, and ''twines'' away her sdaignefull eyes
From his sweet face.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', Godfrey of Boulogne, xx. 128.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To fall.
{{smaller block|<poem>Right on the front he gaue that ladie kinde
A blow so huge, so strong, so great, so sore,
That out of sense and feeling downe she ''twinde''.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', Godfrey of Boulogne, xx. 43.}}}}
'''2.''' To languish; pine away. Probably confused with ''dwine''. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twine-cutter''' (twīn′kut″ėr), ''n.'' A knife or blade, of various form, fixed to a counter, table, stand, etc., to cut the twine used in tying up parcels.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|twin|6553|twine-cutter}}</noinclude>twins are usually polysynthetic, and give rise to a series of fine lines seen on the basal cleavage-face.—'''Baveno twin,''' a kind of twin crystal of orthoclase feldspar, first noted in crystals from Baveno in Italy. The twinning-plane is a clinodome inclined about 45° to the base, and the twin has nearly the form of a square prism.—'''Carlsbad twin,''' a name given to the common twin crystals of orthoclase feldspar often observed in granites, trachytes, and other crystalline rocks, as at Carlsbad in Bohemia. The twinning-axis is here the vertical crystallographic axis, and the twins are commonly of the penetration type.—'''In twin†, a twin†,''' in two; apart.
{{smaller block|<poem>The kyng depertid his pupull, put hom ''in twyn'',
In batels on his best wise for boldyng hym-seluyn.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1181.}}}}
'''Paragenetic twin,''' an ordinary twin crystal in which the compound structure may be considered to belong to it from the beginning of its formation: sometimes used in distinction from ''metagenetic twin'', where the molecular reversal seems to have begun after the crystal had reached a certain development; the latter kind is illustrated by the geniculated twins of rutile.—'''Parasitic twin,''' in ''teratol.'' See ''autosite.''—'''Pericline twin,''' a twin common with the variety of albite called pericline, also with the other triclinic feldspars, where the twinning-axis is the macrodiagonal axis. Such twins are often polysynthetic, and then give a series of striations on the brachydiagonal plane or surface of second cleavage; the direction of these striations varies with the composition of the feldspar according to a definite law.—'''Spinel twin.''' See above, under def. 3.—'''The Siamese twins.''' See ''Siamese.'' —'''The Twins,''' a constellation and sign of the zodiac; Gemini.
{{smaller block|<poem>When now no more ''the'' alternate ''Twins'' are fired</poem>}}
<poem>And Cancer reddens, with the solar blaze,
Short is the doubtful empire of the Night.</poem>{{right|''Thomson'', Summer, l. 43.}}

'''twin<sup>1</sup>''' (twin), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twinned'', ppr. ''twinning''. [< ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To couple; pair; mate; join intimately or link together: said of two united or of one joined to another.
{{smaller block|We were as ''twinn’d'' lambs that did frisk i’ the sun.{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In Gemini that noble power is shown
That ''twins'' their hearts, and doth of two make one.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Hue and Cry.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>                    True liberty
Is lost, which always with right reason dwells
''Twinn’d'', and from her hath no dividual being.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 85.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, in ''mineral.'', to form or unite into a compound or twin crystal by a reversal of the molecular structure according to some definite law.
{{smaller block|Occasionally a simple form is ''twinned'' with a more complex one, as in chabasite. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVI. 363.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be coupled or paired; be mated, as one with another; specifically, to be twin-born.
{{smaller block|<poem>He that is approved in this offence,
Though he had ''twinn’d'' with me, both at a birth,
Shall lose me.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 212.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Were it to plot against the fame, the life
Of one with whom I ''twinned''.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, iii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To bring forth two at a birth.
{{smaller block|Ewes yearly by ''twinning'' rich masters do make.{{right|''Tusser'', January’s Husbandry, st. 28.}}}}

'''twin<sup>2</sup>†''' (twin), ''v.'' [Also ''twine;'' < ME. ''twinnen'', ''twynnen'', lit. go in two (cf. ''in twin'', above), < ''twin'', two: see ''twin''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''twine''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be parted in twain; be divided or sundered; come apart.
{{smaller block|Ther hit onez is tachched, ''twynne'' wil hit neuer.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2512.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My saule, ihesu, take I to thee
When my body and it sal ''twynne.''</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy faith and troth thou sall na get,
And our true love shall never ''twin.''</poem>
{{right|''Clerk Saunders'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 50).}}}}
'''2.''' To part; depart; go away.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fortune wolde that he moste ''twinne''
Out of that place which that I was inne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, l. 569.}}}}
{{smaller block|Loke thou thin herte fro him not ''twynne.''
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}}
'''3.''' To be separated (from) or deprived (of): as, to ''twin'' with one’s gear. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To part in twain; sever; sunder. ''Halliwell.''
{{smaller block|There were twenty and too, to ''twyn'' hom in sonder.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2747.}}}}
{{smaller block|It seith, “Allas! whi ''twynned'' be we tweyne?”
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 679.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When two lovers love each other weel,
Great sin it were them to ''twinn.''</poem>
{{right|''Young Bearwell'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 302).}}}}
'''2.''' To part, as from another person or thing; separate; sunder; especially, to deprive.
{{smaller block|From helle he wille them ''twyn.''
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She’s taen out her little penknife, . . .
And ''twinn’d'' the sweet babe o’ its life.</poem> {{right|''Fine Flowers in the Valley'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 265).}}}}
<poem>Has ''twin’d'' ye o’ your stately trees?”</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Burns'', Destruction of the Woods near Drumlanrig.}}}}

'''twin-born''' (twin′bôrn), ''a.'' Born at the same birth; born along with another.
{{smaller block|<poem>O hard condition,
''Twin-born'' with greatness, subject to the breath
Of every fool!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 1. 251.}}
But such a connection between lordship and land was a slowly developed notion, not a notion ''twin-born'' with the notion of government.
{{right|''W. Wilson'', State, § 15.}}}}

'''twin-cylinder''' (twin′sil″in-dėr), ''a.'' Having twin cylinders: as, a ''twin-cylinder'' engine.

[[File:century v08 p0357 c2f1.png|center|239px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Twin-cylinder Engine.}}}}
{{smaller block|''a'', bed-plate; ''b'', ''b''′, twin cylinders; ''c'', ''c''′, piston-rods; ''d'', ''d''′, guides for piston-rods; ''e'', ''e''′, T-shaped working-beam connected to the piston-rods at ''f'', ''f''′ by slide-blocks pivoted to the ends of the beam and playing in rectangular slideways rigidly attached to the rods. The part ''e''′ of the beam is connected directly with the wrist of a crank on the shaft. The cross-head ''h'' works between the slides ''i'', ''i'', and is pivoted at ''j'' to the beam ''e'', ''e''′; ''k'', eccentric; ''l'', eccentric-strap; ''m'', ''m''′, eccentric-rods; ''n'', ''n''′, rock-shafts which operate the valve-stems ''o'', ''o''′ and the valves.}}

'''twindle''' (twin′dl), ''n.'' [Var. of *''twinnle'', dim. of ''twin''<sup>1</sup>.] A twin. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|In the same book [F. Sparry’s “Geomancie of Maister Christopher Cattan”] the word ''twindle'' (Fr. Gemeaux) occurs for the sign Gemini, two twins in one. Is it known elsewhere?
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 486.}}}}

'''twindle-pippin†''', ''n.'' A double pippin.
{{smaller block|<poem>I dream’d my husband, when he came first a woing,
Came i’ th’ liknes of a Kentish ''twindle-pippen.''</poem>
{{right|''Sampson’s Vow Breaker'' (1636). (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''twine<sup>1</sup>''' (twīn), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''twyne;'' < ME. ''twine'', ''twyne'', ''twin'', double thread, < AS. ''twīn'' (= D. ''twijn;'' cf. Icel. ''tvinni''), a double thread, < ''twi-'', two: see ''twi-''. Cf. ''twin''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A double thread; a thread made of two strands twisted; hence, any coarse strand or cord, or, by extension, a fabric woven of such threads; in modern use, a cord composed of several strands, especially when made of hemp or manila; also, a strong thread made of hemp or cotton, used in sewing sails.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of there hude [hide] he kærf enne thwong, . . .
Nes [nor was] the thwong noht swithe bræd [broad],
Buten swulc a ''twines'' thræd.</poem>
{{right|''Layamon'' (MS. Cott. Calig., A, ix.), l. 14220.}}
<poem>No shetes clene, to lye betwene,
Made of threde and ''twyne.''</poem>
{{right|''The Nut-Brown Maid'' (Percy’s Reliques, II. i. 6).}}}}
'''2.''' The act of twining or twisting; spinning. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>As she some web wrought, or her spindles ''twine''
She cherish’d with her song.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, x. 306.}}}}
'''3.''' A curving, winding, or twisting movement or form; a convolution; a coil; a twist.
{{smaller block|<poem>With an yvie ''twyne'' his waste is girt about.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vi. 14.}}
<poem>Dancing chearely in a siluer ''twine.''</poem>
{{right|''Tourneur'', Trans. Metamorphosis, Epil.}}}}
<poem>Typhon huge ending in snaky ''twine''.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 226.}}

'''4.''' A clasping; an embrace.
{{smaller block|<poem>Milke white leaves, and branches greene,
Folded in amorous ''twines'' together.</poem>{{right|''Heywood'', Prologues and Epilogues (Works, ed. 1874, VI. [352).}}}}

'''5.''' An intertwining or interlacing; a tangle; a snarl.
{{smaller block|<poem>So multiplied were reasons pro and con,
Delicate, intertwisted, and obscure,
That law were shamed to lend a finger-tip
To unravel, readjust the hopeless ''twine''.</poem>{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book.}}}}

'''6†.''' Duality. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Th’ Vnitie dwels in God, ith’ Fiend the ''Twine''.{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Magnificence.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Paper twine''', wrapping-twine made of long, continuous strips of paper, stretched, twisted, and sometimes sized or varnished.}} thread; specifically, consisting or made of twine. See I., 1.

{{smaller block|May live in peace, and rule the land with a ''twine'' thread.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, ii. 1.}}}}

'''Twine cloth''', {{smaller|a fine cotton cloth used as a substitute for linen. Compare ''calico shirting'', under ''shirting''.}}

'''twine<sup>1</sup>''' (twīn), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twined'', ppr. ''twining''. [< ME. ''twinen'', ''twynen'' = D. ''twijnen'' (cf. Icel. ''tvinna'' = Sw. ''tvinna'' = Dan. ''tvinde''), twine, twist, lit. ‘double,’ < AS. ''twin'', a double thread: see ''twine''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make double, as thread, by twisting two strands together; hence, to twist; intertwine.

<poem>To a torche other to a taper the Trinite is likened,
As wexe and a weke were ''twyned'' to-gederes,
And fuyr flaumed forth of hem bothe.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xx. 169.}}}}

{{smaller block|These Rufflers after a year or two at the farthest become Upright men, unless they be prevented by ''twined'' hemp.
{{right|''Harman'', Caveat for Cursetors, p. 15.}}}}

'''2.''' To form of twisted threads or filaments; make by intertwining; in general, to weave.

<poem>Take aff, take aff his costly jupe
(Of gold well was it ''twin’d'').</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Hardyknute'' (Percy’s Reliques, II. i. 17).}}}}

{{smaller block|For the south side [of the tabernacle] southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine ''twined'' linen of an hundred cubits long for one side.
{{right|Ex. xxvii. 9.}}}}

<poem>The Naïads, and the Nymphs, . . .
Upon this joyful day, some dainty chaplets ''twine''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xv. 139.}}}}

'''3.''' To wind or coil about something, as in clasping or embracing it; wreathe; coil.

<poem>She ’s ''twined'' her arms about his waist,
And thrown him into the sea.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''May Colvin'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 274).}}}}
<poem>Fill the Bowl with rosie Wine,
Around our Temples Roses ''twine.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Cowley'', Anacreontics, viii.}}}}

'''4.''' To encircle; entwine; curl around.
{{smaller block|<poem>The plant [Amellus] in holy garlands often ''twines''
The altars’ posts, and beautifies the shrines.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics, iv.}}
<poem>Let wreaths of triumph now my temples ''twine.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., iii. 161.}}}}

'''5.''' To interweave; interlock; intermingle; mix; blend.
{{smaller block|<poem>And all-fore-seeing God in the same Line
Doth oft the god-less with the godly ''twine.''</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Decay.}}
<poem>The child would ''twine''
A trustful hand, unasked, in thine.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cix.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To blend or unite by twisting or winding; intertwine; be interwoven.
{{smaller block|<poem>In ''twining'' hazel bowers.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Sleep’st Thou, or Wak’st Thou?}}
<poem>The light soul ''twines'' and mingles with the growths
Of vigorous early days.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lover’s Tale, i.}}}}

'''2.''' To wind; curl; coil; specifically, of plants, to grow in convolutions about a support. See ''twining.''
{{smaller block|<poem>And, as she runs, the bushes in the way . . .
Some ''twine'' about her thigh to make her stay.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 873.}}
<poem>With the ''twining'' Lash their Shins resound.</poem>
{{right|''Gay'', Trivia, iii. 38.}}
<poem>Aft ha’e I roved by bonnie Doon,
To see the rose and woodbine ''twine.''</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Ye Banks and Braes.}}
A single stick was given to each lot of plants to ''twine'' up. {{right|''Darwin'', Cross and Self Fertilisation, p. 33.}}}} '''3†.''' To warp.
{{smaller block|Because it ''twineth'' and casteth not, it is passing good for hinges and hookes, for sawne bords, for ledges in dores and gates.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xvi. 40.}}}}
'''4.''' To make turns or flexures; wind; meander.
{{smaller block|As rivers, though they bend and ''twine''.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nae gowden stream thro’ myrtles ''twines''.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', On Pastoral Poetry.}}}}

'''twine<sup>2</sup>''' (twīn), ''v.'' [Var. of ''twin''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To separate; divide; part.
{{smaller block|<poem>And sighing says this lady fair,
“They shou’d gar twa loves ''twine''.”</poem>
{{right|''The Water o’ Wearie’s Well'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 200).}}}}
'''2†.''' To turn.
{{smaller block|<poem>She shrikes, and ''twines'' away her sdaignefull eyes
From his sweet face.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', Godfrey of Boulogne, xx. 128.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To fall.
{{smaller block|<poem>Right on the front he gaue that ladie kinde
A blow so huge, so strong, so great, so sore,
That out of sense and feeling downe she ''twinde''.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', Godfrey of Boulogne, xx. 43.}}}}
'''2.''' To languish; pine away. Probably confused with ''dwine''. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twine-cutter''' (twīn′kut″ėr), ''n.'' A knife or blade, of various form, fixed to a counter, table, stand, etc., to cut the twine used in tying up parcels.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
